sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A median in a triangle is a line segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

With that in mind, let's examine our triangles.

  • In triangle I, the line segment [MATH: \overline{CD}] is not a median since [MATH: D] is not the midpoint of [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

  • In triangle II, the line segment [MATH: \overline{CD}] is not a median since [MATH: D] is not the midpoint of [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

  • In triangle III, the line segment [MATH: \overline{CD}] is a median. Indeed, [MATH: D] is the midpoint of [MATH: \overline{AB}.] So, [MATH: \overline{CD}] connects the vertex [MATH: C] with the midpoint [MATH: D] of the opposite side [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

The centroid has an important property that is often called the centroid ratio theorem:

Content:
> The centroid of a triangle splits any median in the proportion [MATH: 2:1,] starting from the corresponding vertex.

Content:
For example, in the diagram below, [MATH: G] is the centroid, and [MATH: \overline{CK}] is one of the medians.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/741048efe529fe60dd996f7aa3747528]

Content:
According to the centroid theorem,
[MATH: CG : GK = 2 : 1.]
The same proportion holds for the other medians of the triangle. Just remember that the longer partition always contains the vertex.

Content:
We'll prove the centroid ratio theorem in a future lesson.

sections.readable_text:
In the diagram below, [MATH: \overline{VL}] and [MATH: \overline{WM}] are medians of [MATH: \triangle UVW.] Find [MATH: GM] given that [MATH: WG=16\: \textrm{cm}.]

[IMG: /graphics/ad86519589fce7c1b319bf7fc2d6dcd4]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
All three medians of a triangle intersect at a point called the centroid of the triangle.

In our case, [MATH: G] is the intersection of the medians [MATH: \overline{VL}] and [MATH: \overline{WM}.] So, [MATH: G] is the centroid.

The centroid of the triangle splits any median in the proportion [MATH: 2:1,] starting from the corresponding vertex.

So, we get that [MATH: WG : GM = 2 : 1.]

Therefore, we have [MATH: GM|= (1)/(2)WG; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 16; = 8cm.]

Content:
The coordinates of a triangle's centroid can be calculated by taking the average of the vertices' [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-coordinates.

Content:
Namely, if [MATH: A(x_A,y_A),] [MATH: B(x_B,y_B),] and [MATH: C(x_C,y_C)] are the coordinates of the vertices of a triangle and [MATH: G(x_G,y_G)] is the centroid, then

Content:
[MATH: x_{G} = (x_{A} + x_{B} + x_{C})/(3), y_{G} = (y_{A} + y_{B} + y_{C})/(3).]

Content:
We'll prove this result in a future lesson. But for now, let's see some examples.

sections.normalized_html: What are the coordinates of the centroid [MATH: G] of [MATH: \triangle PQR.]

What are the coordinates of the centroid [MATH: G] of [MATH: \triangle PQR.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The coordinates of the centroid for a triangle can be calculated by taking the average of the [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-coordinates of the vertices.

In our case, the vertices of the triangle are [MATH: P(-3,1), \qquad Q(4,1), \qquad R(2,5).]

The averages are the following: [MATH: (x_{P} + x_{Q} + x_{R})/(3)|= (− 3 + 4 + 2)/(3) = (3)/(3) = 1; (y_{P} + y_{Q} + y_{R})/(3)|= (1 + 1 + 5)/(3) = (7)/(3)]

Therefore, the centroid is [MATH: G\left(\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}, \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\dfrac 73}\right).]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Centroid Theorem

Content:
Given any triangle, all three medians intersect at a single point called the centroid of the triangle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/90a9cf830d35f9b75ae4c23c242536a6]

Content:
The centroid of a triangle is also its center of mass. In other words, the centroid is where we'd have to place a pencil tip to balance the triangle perfectly.

Content:
More formally, the centroid theorem states the following:

Content:
> For any triangle, the three medians are concurrent, meaning they intersect at a single point. This point of intersection is called the centroid of the triangle.

Content:
We'll prove the centroid theorem in a future lesson.

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Centroid Ratio Theorem

Content:
The centroid has an important property that is often called the centroid ratio theorem:

Content:
> The centroid of a triangle splits any median in the proportion [MATH: 2:1,] starting from the corresponding vertex.

Content:
For example, in the diagram below, [MATH: G] is the centroid, and [MATH: \overline{CK}] is one of the medians.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/741048efe529fe60dd996f7aa3747528]

Content:
According to the centroid theorem,
[MATH: CG : GK = 2 : 1.]
The same proportion holds for the other medians of the triangle. Just remember that the longer partition always contains the vertex.

Content:
We'll prove the centroid ratio theorem in a future lesson.

All three medians of a triangle intersect at a point called the centroid of the triangle.

In our case, [MATH: G] is the intersection of the medians [MATH: \overline{VL}] and [MATH: \overline{WM}.] So, [MATH: G] is the centroid.

The centroid of the triangle splits any median in the proportion [MATH: 2:1,] starting from the corresponding vertex.

So, we get that

Item 14 — Tutorial: Coordinates of the Centroid

Content:
The coordinates of a triangle's centroid can be calculated by taking the average of the vertices' [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-coordinates.

Content:
Namely, if [MATH: A(x_A,y_A),] [MATH: B(x_B,y_B),] and [MATH: C(x_C,y_C)] are the coordinates of the vertices of a triangle and [MATH: G(x_G,y_G)] is the centroid, then

Content:
[MATH: x_{G} = (x_{A} + x_{B} + x_{C})/(3), y_{G} = (y_{A} + y_{B} + y_{C})/(3).]

Content:
We'll prove this result in a future lesson. But for now, let's see some examples.

Item 15 — Example: Finding the Coordinates of a Centroid

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/6b38eb35c9e3423788883b52fb8cfb62]

What are the coordinates of the centroid [MATH: G] of [MATH: \triangle PQR.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The coordinates of the centroid for a triangle can be calculated by taking the average of the [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-coordinates of the vertices.

In our case, the vertices of the triangle are
[MATH: P(-3,1), \qquad
Q(4,1), \qquad
R(2,5).]

The averages are the following:
[MATH: (x_{P} + x_{Q} + x_{R})/(3)|= (− 3 + 4 + 2)/(3) = (3)/(3) = 1; (y_{P} + y_{Q} + y_{R})/(3)|= (1 + 1 + 5)/(3) = (7)/(3)]

Therefore, the centroid is [MATH: G\left(\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}, \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\dfrac 73}\right).]
